questions.question: What most clearly distinguishes likelihood-based generative models from implicit generative models?
questions.choice_A: Likelihood-based models define an explicit probability density and are trained by maximizing (an approximation to) data likelihood, whereas implicit models only define a sampling procedure without a tractable likelihood.
questions.choice_B: Likelihood-based models always require adversarial training, whereas implicit models do not.
questions.choice_C: Implicit models can compute exact likelihoods, whereas likelihood-based models cannot.
questions.choice_D: Implicit models cannot generate high-fidelity samples, whereas likelihood-based models can.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)?
questions.choice_A: They directly minimize the Wasserstein distance between data and model distributions using a discriminator.
questions.choice_B: They optimize a variational lower bound on the log-likelihood that combines a reconstruction term with a KL divergence between the approximate posterior and a prior over latents.
questions.choice_C: They factorize the joint distribution into a product of conditionals and train with teacher forcing.
questions.choice_D: They define an energy function without a normalized probability and rely on MCMC for exact likelihoods.

questions.question: In Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), the core training objective involves:
questions.choice_A: Maximizing exact log-likelihood with respect to a tractable density model.
questions.choice_B: Minimizing reconstruction error between inputs and outputs of a decoder.
questions.choice_C: A minimax game in which a generator tries to fool a discriminator, and the discriminator tries to distinguish real from generated samples.
questions.choice_D: Estimating gradients of the log-density via score matching.

questions.question: A key property of autoregressive models (e.g., PixelCNN, GPT-like decoders) is that they:
questions.choice_A: Use adversarial training to improve perceptual quality at the expense of likelihood.
questions.choice_B: Sample all pixels or tokens in parallel to achieve fast generation.
questions.choice_C: Rely on latent variables and a variational posterior to approximate likelihood.
questions.choice_D: Factorize the joint distribution into a product of conditionals, enabling exact likelihood evaluation but typically slow sequential sampling.

questions.question: Energy-based models (EBMs) are best described as models that:
questions.choice_A: Assign low energy to data and high energy to non-data without requiring a normalized probability, often training with contrastive techniques or MCMC-based negative sampling.
questions.choice_B: Always provide closed-form normalizing constants that make maximum likelihood trivial.
questions.choice_C: Use a discriminator network to approximate Wasserstein distance exactly.
questions.choice_D: Guarantee fast sampling by factorizing the joint distribution.

questions.question: Which statement about maximum likelihood training in generative modeling is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: It primarily optimizes perceptual quality as judged by humans.
questions.choice_B: It encourages covering the full support of the data distribution (reducing mode dropping), but can assign probability mass to unlikely regions, sometimes yielding less sharp samples.
questions.choice_C: It cannot be used with autoregressive models.
questions.choice_D: It guarantees samples indistinguishable from real images.

questions.question: What is "mode collapse" in the context of GANs?
questions.choice_A: The generator produces samples with excessively high noise due to poor likelihood estimation.
questions.choice_B: The discriminator fails to learn, causing the generator to memorize the training set.
questions.choice_C: The generator maps many different latent codes to a small set of outputs, covering only a few modes of the data distribution.
questions.choice_D: A failure mode of MCMC where chains do not mix across modes.

questions.question: Which qualitative trade-off is commonly observed when heavily weighting adversarial loss during training?
questions.choice_A: Improved coverage of rare modes at the expense of sample realism.
questions.choice_B: Exact likelihood estimation with reduced training instability.
questions.choice_C: Faster sampling due to parallel decoding.
questions.choice_D: Higher perceptual fidelity (sharper, more realistic samples) at the risk of reduced diversity and potential mode dropping.

questions.question: Which evaluation pitfall can inflate the Inception Score (IS) without reflecting true generative quality?
questions.choice_A: Generating adversarial or out-of-distribution images that cause the classifier to be overconfident, boosting IS even if samples are not semantically meaningful.
questions.choice_B: Computing IS on synthetic datasets rather than natural images.
questions.choice_C: Using a pretrained classifier trained on the same dataset as the generator.
questions.choice_D: Averaging the score over multiple random seeds.

questions.question: In VAEs, the reconstruction loss primarily encourages:
questions.choice_A: Better mixing behavior in MCMC chains.
questions.choice_B: Decoded outputs that closely match the input data under a chosen likelihood (e.g., pixel-wise), which can lead to blurry reconstructions when combined with strong regularization.
questions.choice_C: The generator to fool a discriminator across multiple scales.
questions.choice_D: Exact matching of the marginal data likelihood without approximation.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the tension between likelihood and perceptual quality?
questions.choice_A: Higher likelihood always implies better human-perceived quality.
questions.choice_B: Lower likelihood guarantees better human-perceived quality.
questions.choice_C: Models like autoregressive decoders can achieve strong likelihoods (low bits-per-dimension) yet produce samples that humans judge as less realistic compared to adversarially trained models.
questions.choice_D: Likelihood and perceptual quality are identical objectives and never diverge.

questions.question: Which evaluation approach is designed to separately assess fidelity and coverage of a generative model?
questions.choice_A: Inception Score (IS) without any modifications.
questions.choice_B: Plain FID computed on a single, small subset of the data.
questions.choice_C: Visual inspection of the top-1 most realistic sample per class.
questions.choice_D: Precision and recall for generative models, which estimate sample quality (precision) and distributional coverage (recall).

questions.question: Why have diffusion-based models gained popularity for image synthesis relative to GANs?
questions.choice_A: They offer more stable training dynamics, strong trade-offs between fidelity and diversity, and reduced susceptibility to mode collapse compared to adversarial training.
questions.choice_B: They compute exact normalized likelihoods with closed-form partition functions.
questions.choice_C: They require no noise or denoising processes during training or sampling.
questions.choice_D: They exclusively optimize adversarial losses, leading to perfect realism.

questions.question: Which statement about the latent representations learned by VAEs is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: They are guaranteed to align with human-interpretable factors without additional constraints.
questions.choice_B: Their structure depends on the choice of prior, encoder capacity, and regularization; without specific inductive biases, semantics are not guaranteed to be disentangled.
questions.choice_C: They cannot be used for conditional generation under any circumstances.
questions.choice_D: They always outperform GAN latents for perceptual quality.

questions.question: How do implicit generative models typically learn without an explicit likelihood?
questions.choice_A: By maximizing cross-entropy with a fixed classifier on real data.
questions.choice_B: By computing exact gradients of the log-likelihood via tractable partition functions.
questions.choice_C: By matching distributions through sample-based objectives, such as adversarial training or minimizing integral probability metrics using a critic/discriminator.
questions.choice_D: By enumerating all modes of the data distribution.

questions.question: Which practice helps detect overfitting or memorization in generative models?
questions.choice_A: Reporting only the best-looking, hand-picked samples in the paper.
questions.choice_B: Computing IS on the training set only.
questions.choice_C: Using a larger batch size during evaluation.
questions.choice_D: Nearest-neighbor analysis in a semantic feature space to check whether generated samples are near-duplicates of training images.

questions.question: Which comparison between autoregressive models and latent-variable models is correct?
questions.choice_A: Autoregressive models provide exact likelihoods via factorization, while latent-variable models often rely on variational bounds (e.g., ELBO) to approximate likelihood.
questions.choice_B: Latent-variable models provide exact likelihoods, while autoregressive models do not.
questions.choice_C: Both require adversarial discriminators for training to be stable.
questions.choice_D: Both always sample in parallel, leading to fast generation.

questions.question: What is a central training challenge for energy-based models?
questions.choice_A: Designing an autoregressive factorization over pixels or tokens.
questions.choice_B: The intractability of the partition function or normalizing constant, which motivates approximate training methods such as contrastive divergence, score matching, or short-run MCMC.
questions.choice_C: The need for paired input-output data to compute reconstruction losses.
questions.choice_D: The impossibility of defining negative samples during training.

questions.question: Which evaluation practice improves the reliability of reported sample quality and diversity?
questions.choice_A: Reporting only curated, cherry-picked samples that look best.
questions.choice_B: Using a single random seed and a small evaluation set to reduce computation.
questions.choice_C: Using random, non-cherry-picked samples; reporting metrics with multiple seeds; and including qualitative analyses like nearest neighbors to rule out memorization.
questions.choice_D: Relying solely on human preference studies without any quantitative metrics.

questions.question: Which observation most clearly indicates mode collapse rather than a likelihood/reconstruction-driven blur?
questions.choice_A: All samples are slightly noisy but cover many categories present in the dataset.
questions.choice_B: Samples are sharp but exhibit artifacts at high frequencies.
questions.choice_C: Reconstructions are uniformly blurry even when conditioned on the same input.
questions.choice_D: Generated outputs are sharp and realistic but concentrate on a few categories or nearly duplicate a small set of training examples, showing poor coverage of the data distribution.
